common_name: Roodnerf Brussels Sprout (Dutch Heirloom Red-Vein Sprout)

planting.note: Start indoors in early summer for a late-fall through winter harvest; Roodnerf is an old Dutch strain selected for cold hardiness and keeps producing sprouts well after hard frost.

directions: Roodnerf is one of the oldest surviving Dutch Brussels sprout strains, distinguished by the reddish-purple tinge running through its leaf veins and stems, a trait that gives the variety its name (Dutch for 'red vein'). It is grown as a traditional late-season sprout, planted in early summer and left to mature slowly into cold weather, since frost exposure sweetens the flavor of the tight, dark-green sprouts. The plants are moderately tall and notably cold-resistant, holding usable sprouts on the stalk from November into February in temperate climates. Because it predates most modern F1 breeding, Roodnerf is more variable in sprout size and uniformity than hybrids, but gardeners value it for its flavor, hardiness, and status as a genetic source behind several later purple-tinged sprout cultivars.
sources: Seeds from Holland — Brussels Sprouts Roodnerf
Real Seed Catalogue — Brussels Sprout Varieties

planting.note: Plant seed potato pieces a few weeks before last frost in cool, workable soil; Eigenheimer is a mid-early floury Dutch heirloom bred in the 1890s.

directions: Eigenheimer was bred in the Netherlands by Geert Veenhuizen in the 1890s from a cross of Blauwe Reuzen and Fransen, and by the 1920s it was the single most widely planted potato in the Dutch countryside, giving its name (literally 'own-home-er', a word for someone who goes their own way) to a whole category of Dutch cultural identity. It produces yellow-fleshed, oval tubers with a dry, floury texture that falls apart readily when boiled, making it a classic choice for mashing and for traditional Dutch stamppot dishes rather than for salads or frying. Plants are mid-early, hilling up twice as foliage develops helps maximize yield and protects developing tubers from sun greening. Eigenheimer has largely been displaced commercially by later Dutch breeding like Bintje, but it remains grown by home gardeners and seed preservation groups for its historic significance and old-fashioned mealy texture.
sources: Potato Research (Springer) — The History of Dutch Potato Breeding 1888–2018
Wageningen University and Research potato cultivar archive

common_name: Noord-Hollandse Bruine Bean (Dutch Brown Soup Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after last frost; this low bush bean needs no staking and is grown through to dry maturity rather than harvested as a snap bean.

directions: Noordhollandse Bruine is the traditional home-garden strain of the Dutch brown bean, a compact, non-climbing bush type long grown in North Holland and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen for the caramel-brown dry beans used in bruine bonensoep, the classic Dutch brown bean soup eaten with smoked sausage. Plants stay low and need no support, setting slender pods around 3.5 inches long that can be eaten fresh and snapped like a green bean when young, but are more commonly left on the plant until the pods dry and the oval, yellow-brown beans rattle loose inside. Because the bean was historically considered humble peasant food, it fell out of commercial favor compared to white and kidney types, but home gardeners still prize its rich, nutty flavor and the way the cooked beans hold their shape rather than turning mushy. Let pods dry fully on the plant before shelling, then store the dried beans in a sealed container for soups and stews through winter.

common_name: Liège Giant Winter Leek (Belgian Heirloom Winter Leek)

planting.note: Start indoors well ahead of the season, since this is a slow-growing winter leek meant to stand in the ground through hard frost; transplant out once seedlings are pencil-thick.

directions: Liège Giant Winter is an old Belgian heritage leek from the Liège region of eastern Belgium, grown by home gardeners there as a hardy winter standby rather than a quick-maturing summer crop. It forms thick, long shanks under dark, blue-green foliage and is prized above all for its exceptional cold tolerance, able to stand in the garden through hard freezes without turning to mush, so it can be harvested fresh through the depths of winter instead of being pulled and stored. Hilling soil or mulch up around the developing shank as the plant grows lengthens the tender white portion and shields it from sun and frost damage alike. This is a leek for patient gardeners in cold climates who want a late-fall through winter harvest of thick, sweet shanks once milder-climate leeks have already finished.
sources: Adaptive Seeds — Leek, Liège Giant Winter
ILVO (Flanders Research Institute for Agriculture) — Breeding potential of Belgian landraces of leek

common_name: Hersbrucker Spät Hop (Franconian Bavarian Landrace Hop)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in deep, fertile soil after last frost; this late-maturing Franconian landrace needs a longer season than earlier noble hops before cones are ready.

directions: Hersbrucker Spät takes its name from the small Franconian town of Hersbruck near Nuremberg, at the northern edge of Bavaria's hop country, where it developed as a farmer-selected landrace long before formal hop breeding existed. It became one of Germany's most important aroma hops in the 19th century and saw renewed importance in the mid-20th century for its strong resistance to Verticillium wilt, a disease that devastated other traditional German hopyards. True to its name, it is a late-maturing variety, so growers should expect cones to finish well after earlier noble types, with a delicate, slightly floral and fruity aroma profile that is the traditional choice for unfiltered Franconian kellerbier. Give it the same tall, sturdy trellis, full sun, and deep, well-drained soil that any noble hop needs, and watch for downy mildew, to which the variety is somewhat more susceptible than to other common hop diseases.
sources: Yakima Chief Hops — Hersbrucker Spät variety data

common_name: Spalter Select Hop (Bavarian Noble Aroma Hop)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in deep, fertile soil after last frost; bred as a sturdier replacement for the traditional Spalt landrace, it establishes more reliably than older noble hops.

directions: Spalter Select was bred at the Hop Research Center in Hüll, Bavaria, released in 1993 from a cross of the old Spalt landrace with Hallertauer Mittelfrüh, with the explicit goal of giving growers around the historic hop town of Spalt a more productive, disease-resistant alternative to the fragile traditional landrace. It carries forward the fine, spicy-floral character that made Spalt one of Germany's protected noble hop designations, with a touch more spice in the aroma than its parent. Because it yields and establishes more reliably than true heirloom Spalt, it is a more forgiving choice for home growers who still want an authentic Bavarian noble hop character in pilsners and German-style lagers. Provide the tall trellis, full sun, and rich, well-drained soil all noble hops need, and expect modest yields in the planting's first year with full production by the third season.

common_name: Schwetzinger Meisterschuss Asparagus (Historic South German White Asparagus)

planting.note: Plant crowns in deep, sandy, mounded ridges so spears can be earthed up and cut while still blanched white, in the traditional South German style.

directions: Schwetzinger Meisterschuss traces its lineage to the breeding work of palace garden master Gustav Unselt in Schwetzingen, Baden, beginning around 1911, with the named variety itself released in 1952; Schwetzingen has been Germany's best-known asparagus town since the early 1900s, when 'Meisterschuss' and the related 'Lukullus' first made its reputation. Unlike modern all-male hybrids bred for uniformity, Meisterschuss is an older-style mixed-sex, open-pollinated variety, medium-early to crop and vigorous once established, though it has become rare in commercial production as hybrids have taken over. Mound soil over the crowns each spring to grow the pale, mild spears prized in traditional South German Spargel cookery, and expect more variable spear thickness than a modern hybrid delivers. This is a variety for gardeners and small growers who want a living piece of Germany's asparagus history alongside their harvest.
